translations.text: After Saul’s death, David returned from defeating the Amalekites and stayed in Ziklag for two days.
After the second day, a man arrived from the camp of Saul’s army, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. When he came to David, he fell to the ground and bowed before him.
David said to him, “Where have you come from?” He said to him, “I have escaped from the camp of Israel.”
David said to him, “What is the news? Tell me.” He said, “The people fled from the battle, and many of the people fell and died. Saul and Jonathan also died.”
David said to the young man who had brought him the news, “How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?”
The young man who had brought him the news said, “I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, leaning on his spear. Chariots and mounted warriors were closing in on him.
He looked behind him, saw me, and called to me. I said, ‘Here I am.’
He said to me, ‘Who are you?’ I said, ‘I am an Amalekite.’
He said to me, ‘Come over me and kill me, for a terrible darkness has seized me, though all my life is still in me.’
So I stood over him and killed him, because I knew that he would not survive after his fall. I took the crown from his head and the bracelets from his arm and brought them here to my lord.”
David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and all the men who were with him tore their clothes.
They mourned, fasted, and wept until evening for Saul and his son Jonathan, for the people of Judah, and for the house of Israel, because they had been struck down by the sword.
David said to the young man who had brought him the news, “Where are you from?” He said, “I am the son of an Amalekite who lives as a foreigner.”
David said to him, “How were you not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy the Lord’s anointed?”
David called one of the young men and said, “Come forward and strike him down.” He struck him, and he died.
David said to him, “Your blood is on your own head, because your own mouth testified against you, saying, ‘I killed the Lord’s anointed.’”
David sang this lament over Saul and his son Jonathan.
David said that the sons of Judah should be taught archery. It is written in the Book of Jashar.
Stand still, Israel, over the wounded on your hills, on your heights! How the mighty have fallen!
Do not tell it in Gath, and do not announce this news in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the foreigners rejoice and the daughters of the uncircumcised celebrate.
Mountains of Gilboa, let no dew fall on you, nor rain come upon you, nor fields bear fruit. For there the shield of the mighty was defiled; Saul’s shield was not anointed with oil.
From the blood of the wounded and the fat of the mighty, Jonathan’s bow did not turn back empty, and Saul’s sword was not sheathed empty.
Saul and Jonathan were loved, beautiful, and gracious, not separated in their lives, nor separated in their death. They were swifter than eagles and stronger than lions.
Daughters of Israel, weep for Saul! Weep for him who clothed you in scarlet with your finery, who put ornaments of gold on your clothes.
How the mighty have fallen in the midst of battle! Jonathan lies wounded on your heights.
I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan. You were very dear to me. Your love for me was more wonderful than the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!
After this, David inquired of the Lord, saying, “Shall I go up to one of the cities of Judah?” The Lord said to him, “Go up.” David said, “Where shall I go up?” He said, “To Hebron.”
David went up to Hebron with both his wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel.
And the men whom David brought up, each with his own household, camped in the city of Hebron.
And the men of Judea came and anointed David there as king over the house of Judah. And they told David, saying, “The men of Jabesh-gilead buried Saul.”

And David sent messengers to the leaders of Jabesh-gilead, and David said to them, “You are blessed by the Lord, because you showed this kindness to your lord Saul, the Lord’s anointed, and buried him and Jonathan his son.
And now may the Lord show you mercy and faithfulness, and I too will repay you for this kindness, because you have done this thing.”
Now let your hands be strong, and be valiant men, for your lord Saul has died, and the house of Judah has anointed me as their king.
And Abner son of Ner, Saul’s commander, took Ish-bosheth son of Saul and brought him to the camp.
And he made him king over Gilead, over Thasira, over Jezreel, over Ephraim, over Benjamin, and over all Israel.
And Ish-bosheth son of Saul was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he reigned for two years, except over the house of Judah, who followed David.
And the time during which David reigned in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.
And Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul went out from the camps to Gibeon.
And Joab son of Zeruiah and David’s servants went out from Hebron and met them at the spring of Gibeon. They sat on that side of the spring of Gibeon, and these sat on this side.
And Abner said to Joab, “Let the young men rise and compete before us.” And Joab said, “Let them rise.”
They rose and went across, twelve in number from the young men of Benjamin belonging to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve from David’s young men.
And each man seized his opponent’s head with his hand and thrust his sword into his opponent’s side, and they fell and died there. And that place was named the Portion of Traitors; it is in Gibeon.
And there was a very fierce battle that day, and Abner and the men of Israel were defeated before David’s servants.
And the three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. And Asahel was swift-footed, like one of the gazelles in the field.
And Asahel pursued Abner closely and did not turn aside to the right or to the left from following Abner.
And Abner looked behind him and said, “Is that you, Asahel?” And he said, “It is I.”
And Abner said to him, “Turn aside to the right or to the left, seize one of the young men, and take his armor for yourself.” But Asahel would not turn aside from following him.
And Abner again said to Asahel, “Stay away from me, so that I do not strike you to the ground. How could I lift my face toward Joab? And where would that leave us? Return to your brother Joab.”

But he would not withdraw, and Abner struck him in the belly with his spear, and the spear came out through his hip. He fell there and died beneath him. And everyone who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died stood still.
And Joab and Abishai pursued Abner closely. The sun set, and they came as far as the hill of Ammah, which is opposite Giah, along the road to the wilderness of Gibeon.
And the sons of Benjamin gathered behind Abner and stood on top of a hill.

And Abner called to Joab and said, “Will the sword devour completely? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? How long will you refrain from telling the people to turn back from pursuing their brothers?”
And Joab said, “As the Lord lives, if you had not spoken, the crowd would have gone away this morning, each following his brother.”
And Joab blew the trumpet, and all the people withdrew. They no longer pursued Israel and did not continue fighting.
Abner and his men traveled eastward all that night, crossed the Jordan, went through the whole stretch of land, and came to the camp.
Joab returned from pursuing Abner and gathered all the people. When David’s servants were counted, nineteen men and Asahel had been killed.
David’s servants had struck down three hundred and sixty men from among the Benjaminites and Abner’s men.
They carried Asahel away and buried him in his father’s tomb in Bethlehem. Joab and his men traveled on, and dawn found them in Hebron.
There was fierce warfare between the house of Saul and the house of David. The house of David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker.
Sons were born to David in Hebron: his firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel;
his second was Davia, by Abigail of Carmel; and his third was Absalom, by Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur;
his fourth was Adonijah, the son of Haggith; and his fifth was Shephatiah, the son of Amital;
and his sixth was Ithream, by David’s wife Eglah. These were born to David in Hebron.
While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was in control of the house of Saul.
Saul had a concubine named Rizpah, the daughter of Juga. Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, said to Abner, “Why do you go in to my father’s concubine?”

Abner became very angry at Ish-bosheth’s words and said to him, “Am I a dog’s head? To this day I have shown kindness to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers, and to his friends, and I have not surrendered to the house of David. Yet today you seek to punish me over a woman!
May God do this and more to Abner if I do not do for David just as the Lord swore to him:
to take away Saul’s kingdom and establish David’s kingdom over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.”
Ish-bosheth could no longer answer Abner a single word, because he was afraid.
Abner immediately sent messengers to David in the land of Thesalmu, saying, “Make your covenant with me, and my hand will be with you to bring the whole house of Israel over to you.”
David said, “Good. I will make a covenant with you. But I ask one thing of you: you must not see my face unless you bring Michal, Saul’s daughter, when you come to see me.”
David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, saying, “Give me my wife Michal, whom I married in exchange for a hundred foreskins of the foreigners.”
Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband Paltiel, the son of Sella.
Her husband followed her, weeping, as far as Bahurim. Abner said to him, “Go back.” And he went back.
Abner spoke with the elders of Israel and said, “In the past you sought to have David reign over you.
Now do it, for the Lord has spoken concerning David, saying, ‘By the hand of my servant David I will save Israel from the hands of the Philistines and from the hands of all their enemies.’”
Abner also spoke to the Benjaminites. Then Abner went to speak to David in Hebron about everything that seemed good to Israel and to the whole house of Benjamin.
Abner came to David in Hebron with twenty men. David made a feast for Abner and the men who were with him.

Abner said to David, “I will arise and go and gather all Israel to my lord the king, and I will make a covenant with you. You will reign over all whom your heart desires.” David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.
Then David’s servants and Joab came back from a raid, bringing much plunder with them. Joab was not with David in Hebron when he sent him away and he went in peace.
Joab and all his army arrived, and Joab was informed: “Abner son of Ner came to David, and he sent him away, and he went in peace.”
Joab went in to King David and said, “What have you done? Abner came to you, and why did you send him away in peace?
Do you not know the wickedness of Abner son of Ner? He came to deceive you, to learn your comings and goings, and to find out everything you do.”
Joab left David and sent messengers after Abner. They brought him back from the well of Sirah, but David did not know.
He brought Abner back to Hebron, and Joab took him aside at the gate to speak with him treacherously. He struck him in the belly, and he died because of the blood of Asahel, Joab’s brother.
David heard about it afterward and said, “I and my kingdom are forever innocent before the Lord of the blood of Abner son of Ner.

May it fall upon Joab’s head and upon his father’s entire household. May Joab’s household never lack someone with a discharge, a leper, a beggar who walks with a staff, someone who dies by the sword, or someone who dies of hunger.”
Joab and his brother Abishai lay in wait for Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel in the battle at Gibeon.
David said to Joab and to all the people with him, “Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn before Abner.” King David walked behind the bier.
They buried Abner in Hebron. The king raised his voice and wept over his grave, and all the people wept over Abner.
The king took up a lament over Abner and said, “Did Abner die as a fool dies? Did Abner die the death of Nabal?

Your hands were not bound, and your feet were not entangled in chains. You were not delivered up like Nabal before wicked men and fell; rather, you fell as people fall before the unjust.” And all the people gathered to weep for him.
All the people came to give David food while it was still day. But David swore and said, “May God do so and so to me, and add still more, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets.”
All the people understood, and everything the king did seemed pleasing to them; they regarded it as good.
All the people and all Israel understood that day that the killing of Abner son of Ner had not come from the king.
The king said to his servants, “Do you not know that a great leader has fallen in Israel today?
And he is a kinsman today and has been appointed by the king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are harsher than I am. May the Lord repay the evildoer according to his wickedness.”
When Ish-bosheth son of Saul heard that Abner had died in Hebron, his hands grew weak, and all the men of Israel lost heart.

There were two men who commanded the troops of Ish-bosheth son of Saul. One was named Baanah and the other Rechab. They were sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, from the descendants of Benjamin, for Beeroth too was counted among the descendants of Benjamin.
The Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have lived there as foreigners to this day.

Jonathan son of Saul had a son who was disabled in his feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and his son Jonathan arrived from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and fled, and as she hurried to escape, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.
Rechab and Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, went and entered Ish-bosheth’s house during the heat of the day, while he was sleeping on his bed at midday.
The gatekeeper of the house was cleaning wheat, became drowsy, and fell asleep. And the brothers Rechab and Baanah slipped in unnoticed.
They entered the house, and Ish-bosheth was asleep on his bed in his chamber. They struck him and killed him, cut off his head, took the head, and traveled along the eastern road all night.

They brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron and said to the king, “Here is the head of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. Today the Lord has given our lord the king vengeance on his enemies—on Saul, your enemy, and on his offspring.”
David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said to them, “As the Lord lives, who rescued my life from every distress,
when someone told me, ‘Saul is dead,’ and thought he was bringing me good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag, though I would have been expected to give him a reward for his news.
And now you wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house, on his bed. Now I will demand his blood from your hands and destroy you from the earth.”

David gave orders to his young men, and they killed them, cut off their hands and feet, and hung them beside the pool at Hebron. They buried the head of Ish-bosheth in the tomb of Abner son of Ner at Hebron.
All the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, “Look, we are your bone and your flesh.
In times past, while Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them in. The Lord said to you, ‘You shall shepherd my people Israel, and you shall be ruler over Israel.’”
All the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron. King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the Lord, and they anointed David king over all Israel.
David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned for forty years.
He reigned over Judah at Hebron for seven years and six months, and he reigned over all Israel and Judah at Jerusalem for thirty-three years.

David and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites who lived in the land. David was told, “You will not enter here, for the blind and the lame have opposed you and say, ‘David must not enter here.’”
David captured Zion and its stronghold, which is the City of David.

David said that day, “Anyone who strikes the Jebusites with the sword and attacks with the sword both the lame and the blind, those whom David hates.” That is why they say, “The blind and the lame must not enter the house of the Lord.”
David lived in the stronghold, and it was called the City of David. David built it up as a city all around, from end to end, and built his own house.
David continued to grow greater, and the Lord Almighty was with him.
Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, along with fir timber, carpenters, and stonemasons, and they built a house for David.
David knew that the Lord had established him as king over Israel and that his kingdom had been exalted for the sake of his people Israel.
David took more wives and concubines from Jerusalem after leaving Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David.
These are the names of the sons born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon [?],
Ibhar, Elishua, Eliphelet, Nogah, Nepheg,
Jonathan, Elishama, Baal-iada [?], and Eliphelet.
The Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, and all the Philistines went up to seek David. David heard about it and went down to the stronghold.
The Philistines came and gathered in the valleys of the giants.

David inquired of the Lord, saying, “Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you deliver them into my hands?” The Lord said to David, “Go up, for I will certainly deliver the Philistines into your hands.”

David came to Above the Breaches and defeated the Philistines there. David said, “The Lord has broken through my enemies before me, as water breaks through.” Therefore that place was named Above the Breaches.
They left their gods there, and David and the men with him took them.
The Philistines came up again and gathered in the Valley of the Giants.

David inquired of the Lord, saying, “Shall I go up against the Philistines, and will you deliver them into my hands?” The Lord said, “Do not go up against them. Turn away from them and come against their flank near the weeping trees.
When you hear the sound of movement in the grove of weeping trees, then go down against them, for then the Lord will go out before you to strike down the Philistines in battle.”
David did as the Lord commanded him, and he struck down the Philistines from Gibeon as far as Gezer.
David again gathered all the young men of Israel, about seventy thousand.

David arose and went, with all his people accompanying him, from the rulers of Judah to the ascent by which the ark of God went up. Over it was invoked the name of the Lord God of hosts, who sits upon the cherubim above it.
He brought out the ark of the Lord and placed it on a new cart.
He took it from the house of Abinadab, who lived on the hill. Uzzah and his brothers, the sons of Abinadab, drove the cart carrying the ark, and his brothers walked ahead of the ark.
David and the Israelites celebrated before the Lord with harps and musical instruments, with vigor and songs, and with lyres, flutes, tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets.
They came as far as Abinadab’s threshing floor, and Uzzah stretched out his hand toward the ark of God to hold it and took hold of it, because the ox had tilted it away from its support.
The Lord was angry with Uzzah, and God struck him there for his presumption. He died there beside the ark of the Lord, before God.
David was distressed because the Lord had broken out against Uzzah, and that place has been called the Breach of Uzzah to this day.
David feared the Lord that day and said, “How can the ark of God come to me?”
David did not wish to bring the ark of the Lord’s covenant to himself in the City of David. Instead, David diverted it to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.
The ark of the Lord remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the Lord blessed Obed-edom and his entire household.

They told David, saying, “The Lord has blessed the house of Obed-edom and everything belonging to him because of the ark of God.” David went and brought the ark of the Lord up from the house of Obed-edom to the City of David with rejoicing.
With him were those carrying the ark, seven companies of dancers, and a sacrifice of an ox and lambs.
David played the musical harps before the Lord, and David was dressed in a robe [?].
David and the whole house of Israel brought up the ark of the Lord with shouting and the sound of a trumpet.
As the ark reached the City of David, Michal, Saul’s daughter, looked through the window and saw King David dancing and playing musical instruments before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart.
They brought the ark of the Lord and set it in its place inside the tent David had pitched for it. David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord.
When David had finished offering the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord of hosts.

He distributed to all the people, to the whole assembly of Israel from Dan to Beersheba, to men and women alike, a loaf of bread, a portion of roasted meat, and a cake from the frying pan for each person. Then all the people went away, each to their own home.

David returned to bless his household, and Michal, Saul’s daughter, came out to meet David. She blessed him and said, “How glorious the king of Israel was today, uncovering himself today before his maidservants and servants, just as one of the dancers openly uncovers himself!”

David said to Michal, “I will dance before the Lord. Blessed is the Lord God, who chose me rather than your father or anyone in his household and appointed me ruler over his people Israel. I will rejoice and dance before the Lord.
I will uncover myself even more than this, and I will be worthless in your eyes. But among the maidservants you spoke of, I will indeed be honored.”
Michal, Saul’s daughter, had no child until the day of her death.
And it happened, when David was settled in his house and the Lord had given him rest from all his enemies around him,
The king said to Nathan the prophet, “Look, I live in a house of fir wood, while the ark of God moves about within a tent.”
Nathan said to the king, “Go and do whatever is in your heart, for the Lord is with you.”
That night the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying:
“Go and tell my servant David: ‘This is what the Lord says: You shall not build me a house to live in.
For I have not lived in a house from the day I brought the children of Israel out of Egypt until today, but I have moved about with a tent as my lodging.
Wherever I moved about among all Israel, did I ever speak to any tribe of Israel that I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, “Why have you not built me a house of fir wood?”’
Now say this to my servant David: ‘This is what the Lord Almighty says: I took you from the sheepfolds to be ruler over my people Israel.
I was with you wherever you went, and I destroyed all your enemies before you. I made your name famous, like the names of the great ones on earth.
I will appoint a place for my people Israel and plant them there. They will live on their own and no longer be troubled, and no son of lawlessness will oppress them again as before,
from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel. I will give you rest from all your enemies, and the Lord will tell you that you shall build him a house.
When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish your kingdom for him.
He will build a house for my name, and I will establish his throne forever.
I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me. If wrongdoing arises in him, I will rebuke him and discipline him with the rod of men and with the punishments of the sons of men.
But I will not withdraw my mercy from him, as I withdrew it from those who rejected [?] before me.
His name and his kingdom shall remain secure before me forever, and his throne shall stand firm before me forever.’”
Nathan spoke to David according to all these words and this entire vision.
King David went in and sat before the Lord and said, “Who am I, my Lord God, and what is my household, that you have loved me this far?
And I was not humbled at all before you, Lord, my Lord, and you spoke at length concerning the house of your servant. Is this the law of humanity, Lord, my Lord?
What more can David say to you? You yourself know your servant, my Lord God.
For your servant’s sake, and according to all that is in your heart, you have done all this great work, making it known to your servant,
to make me great, my Lord God. For there is no one like you, and there is no God besides you, according to everything we have heard with our ears.

And what nation on earth is like your people Israel, whom God led in order to redeem as his own people, to make a name for yourself and bring about greatness and revelation for yourself, driving out before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, nations and their settlements?
And you established your people Israel for yourself as a people forever, and you, Lord, became their God.
Now, my Lord, establish forever the word you spoke concerning your servant and his house, and do as you have said.
And may your name be magnified forever. And now the Lord Almighty is God over all Israel. May the house of your servant David stand firm before you.

For you are the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel. And now, as you have spoken, may your name be magnified forever, says the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel. You revealed this in the hearing of your servant and said, “I will build you a house.” Therefore your servant found the courage to stand before you in prayer and offer these prayers.
And now, my Lord God, you are God, and your words shall be true, and you have spoken of all this goodness concerning your servant.

And now begin to bless the house of your servant, so that it may remain before you forever. For you, my Lord God, have spoken, and through your blessing the house of your servant shall be blessed forever.
And after this David struck the Philistines and drove them back, and David took from the Philistines what had been set apart.

And David struck Moab and measured them with cords, making them lie down on the ground. Two lengths of cord were for those to be killed, and two lengths of cord were for those to be kept alive. And Moab became David’s servants, bringing tribute.
And David struck Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to extend his power over the Euphrates River.
And David took from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand foot soldiers. David dismantled all the chariots but kept a hundred chariots for himself.
And the Syrians came from Damascus to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, and David struck down twenty-two thousand men among the Syrians.
David placed garrisons in Syria opposite Damascus, and the Syrians became David’s servants, bringing tribute. The Lord delivered David wherever he went.
And David took the gold armlets that were on the servants of Hadadezer king of Zobah and brought them to Jerusalem.

And Shishak king of Egypt took these when he came up to Jerusalem in the days of Rehoboam son of Solomon. And from Masbaca, from the choicest cities of Hadadezer, King David took bronze, with which Solomon made the bronze Sea, the pillars, the basins, and all the furnishings.
And Toi king of Hamath heard that David had struck down all Hadadezer’s army.

And Toi sent his son Jaddura to King David to ask about his welfare, and he blessed him because he had destroyed Hadadezer. For Hadadezer was a fierce warrior against Toi and stood in opposition to him. And Jaddura brought gold vessels, silver vessels, and bronze vessels.
And King David dedicated these to the Lord, together with the silver and gold that he had dedicated from all the wars in which he had been victorious:
from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and the spoils of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
And David made a name for himself, and on his return David struck down eighteen thousand Syrians at Gabeghem.
And he placed garrisons in Edom, among all the Edomites, and all the Edomites became servants of the king. And the Lord delivered David wherever he went.
And he made David king over all Israel, and David administered justice and righteousness for all his people.
And Joab son of Zeruiah was in command of the army, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahijah was in charge of the records.
And Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests, and Asa was chief scribe.
And Benaiah son of Jehoiada was an adviser, and the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and David’s sons were chief officials.
David said, “Is there anyone left from the house of Saul, so that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
There was a servant from Saul’s household named Ziba. They called him to David, and the king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” He said, “I am your servant.”
The king said, “Is there anyone left from Saul’s household to whom I may show the kindness of God?” Ziba said to the king, “There is a son of Jonathan who is disabled in his feet.”
The king said, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “He is in the house of Machir son of Ammiel, of Lo-debar.”
King David sent and brought him from the house of Machir son of Ammiel, of Lo-debar.
Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to King David, fell on his face, and bowed before him. David said to him, “Mephibosheth!” He said, “Here I am, your servant.”

David said to him, “Do not be afraid, for I will certainly show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the fields of Saul, your grandfather, and you will always eat bread at my table.”
Mephibosheth bowed and said, “Who is your servant, that you have taken notice of a dead dog like me?”
The king called Ziba, Saul’s servant, and said to him, “I have given everything belonging to Saul and everything belonging to his household to your master’s son.”

“You, your sons, and your servants shall work the land for him, and you shall bring food into your master’s house, and they shall eat it. But Mephibosheth, your master’s son, shall always eat bread at my table.” Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba said to the king, “Your servant will do everything that my lord the king has commanded his servant.” And Mephibosheth ate bread at David’s table like one of the king’s sons.
Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica, and all the members of Ziba’s household were Mephibosheth’s servants.
Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king’s table. He was lame in both feet.
After this, the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun reigned in his place.

David said, “Let us show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” David sent his servants to comfort him over the loss of his father, and David’s servants went to the land of the Ammonites.

The Ammonite leaders said to Hanun their lord, “Was it really to honor your father before you that David sent comforters to you? No, David sent his servants to you to search out this city, inspect it, and spy on it.”
He seized David’s servants, shaved off their beards, cut their [?] through the middle down to the edge, and sent them away.
David was told about the men, and he sent to meet them, because the men had been greatly disgraced. The king said, “Stay in Jericho until your beards grow, and then return.”

When the Ammonites saw that they had disgraced David’s people, they sent and hired the Arameans of Rehob and the Arameans of Zobah, twenty thousand foot soldiers, the king of Amalek with a thousand men, and twelve thousand men from Tob.
King David heard and sent Joab and the whole force of mighty warriors.
The Ammonites came out and drew up for battle at the city gate. The Arameans of Zobah and Rehob, and those of Tob and Amalek, were by themselves in the open country.
Joab saw that they had come upon him from the front and from behind. He chose men from among all the young men of Israel and drew them up against the Arameans.
He placed the rest of the army under the command of his brother Abishai, and they drew up against the Ammonites.
And he said, “If the Syrians overpower me, you must come to my rescue; and if the Ammonites overpower you, we will come to rescue you.”
“Be strong, and let us act courageously for our people and for the cities of our God. May the Lord do what is pleasing in his eyes.”
Joab and the troops with him advanced into battle against the Syrians, and the Syrians fled before him.
When the Ammonites saw that the Syrians had fled, they too fled before Abishai and entered the city. Joab withdrew from the Ammonites and returned to Jerusalem.
When the Syrians saw that they had been defeated before Israel, they gathered together.
Hadadezer sent and gathered the Syrians from beyond the River to Chalamak. Helam and Shobach, commanders of Hadadezer’s forces, arrived ahead of him.
David was informed, and he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and arrived at Chalamak. The Syrians drew up their battle lines against David to fight him.
The Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed seven hundred chariot crews and forty thousand horsemen of the Syrians. He also struck Shobach, the commander of their army, and he died there.

When all the kings who served Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated before Israel, they surrendered, made a covenant with Israel, and served them. From then on, the Syrians were afraid to come to the rescue of the Ammonites.

At the turn of the year, at the time when kings go out to war, David sent Joab, his servants with him, and all Israel. They destroyed the Ammonites and laid siege to Rabbah, while David remained in Jerusalem.
One evening, David rose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful.
David sent to inquire about the woman, and someone said, “Is this not Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliab, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”
David sent messengers and took her. She came to him, and he slept with her. She had purified herself from her menstrual period, and she returned to her house.
The woman conceived and sent word to David, saying, “I am pregnant.”
David sent word to Joab, saying, “Send Uriah the Hittite to me.” And Joab sent Uriah to David.
Uriah came into David’s presence, and David asked how Joab was, how the army was, and how the war was going.
Uriah said, “All is well.” David said to Uriah, “Go down to your house and wash your feet.” Uriah left the king’s house, and a gift from the king followed him.
Uriah slept at the entrance of the king’s house with his servants and did not go down to his own house.
They told David, saying, “Uriah did not go down to his house.” David said to Uriah, “Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?”

Uriah said to David, “The ark of God and Israel and Judah are staying in tents, and my lord Joab and my lord’s servants are camping in the open. Shall I go into my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? How could that be? As surely as you live, I will not do such a thing.”
David said to Uriah, “Stay here today, and tomorrow I will send you away.” So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him, and he ate and drank in his presence and became drunk. Late in the evening he went out and slept on his bed with his lord’s servants, but he did not go down to his own house.
In the morning, David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.
He wrote in the letter, saying, “Put Uriah at the front where the fighting is fiercest, and withdraw from him so that he may be struck down and die.”
While Joab was keeping watch over the city, he placed Uriah where he knew there were mighty warriors.
The men of the city came out to fight against Joab, and some of the troops of David’s servants fell and died. Uriah the Hittite also died.
Joab sent word and reported to the king everything that had happened in the battle.
He instructed the messenger, saying, “When you have finished telling the king everything that happened in this battle,
if the king’s anger rises and he says to you, ‘Why did you go near the city to fight? Did you not know that they shoot arrows from above, from the walls?’”

Who struck Abimelech, the son of Jerubbaal, the son of Ner? Did not a woman throw a piece of a millstone down on him from the top of the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you approach the wall? Then you shall say, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite also died.’

Joab’s messenger went to the king in Jerusalem. He arrived and told David everything Joab had instructed him to tell, all the events of the battle. David became angry with Joab and said to the messenger, “Why did you go near the city to fight? Did you not know that you would be struck from the wall? Who struck Abimelech son of Jerubbaal? Was it not a woman who threw a piece of a millstone down on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go near the wall?”
The messenger said to David, “The men pressed hard against us and came out against us in the open, but we drove them back as far as the city gate.
Then the archers shot at your servants from above, from the wall, and some of the king’s servants died. Your servant Uriah the Hittite also died.”

David said to the messenger, “Say this to Joab: ‘Do not let this matter seem bad in your eyes, for the sword devours sometimes one way and sometimes another. Press the battle harder against that city and destroy it, and take courage.’”
When Uriah’s wife heard that her husband Uriah had died, she mourned for her husband.
When the mourning was over, David sent for her and brought her into his house. She became his wife and bore him a son. But what David had done was evil in the eyes of the Lord.
The Lord sent Nathan the prophet to David. He came to him and said, “There were two men in a certain city, one rich and the other poor.
The rich man had very many flocks and herds,

but the poor man had nothing except one little ewe lamb, which he had bought, kept alive, and raised. It had grown up with him and his children together. It ate his bread, drank from his cup, and slept in his arms, and it was like a daughter to him.

A traveler came to the rich man, but he spared his own flocks and herds rather than taking from them to prepare a meal for the traveler who had come to him. Instead, he took the poor man’s ewe lamb and prepared it as food for the man who had come to him.”
David became intensely angry with the man and said to Nathan, “As the Lord lives, the man who did this deserves to die!
He must repay sevenfold for the ewe lamb because he did this thing and showed no pity.”
Nathan said to David, “You are the man who did this! This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over all Israel, and I rescued you from the hands of Saul.
I gave you your master’s house and your master’s wives into your arms. I gave you Israel and Judah, and if that were too little, I would have added as much again for you.
Why did you despise the word of the Lord by doing evil in his sight? You struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife to be your wife. You killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.
Now the sword will never depart from your house, because you despised me and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.

This is what the Lord says: Look, I will raise up trouble against you from your own house. I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he will sleep with your wives in the sight of this sun.’”
For you did this in secret, but I will do this thing in the sight of all Israel and before this sun.
David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the Lord.” Nathan said to David, “The Lord has also taken away your sin; you will not die.”
But because by this deed you have greatly provoked the Lord’s enemies, the son who is to be born to you shall surely die.
Then Nathan went to his house, and the Lord struck the child whom Uriah’s wife had borne to David, and he became ill.
David pleaded with God for the child. David fasted, went in, and lay on the ground.
The servants of his household stood over him to raise him up, but he would not rise from the ground or eat bread with them.

On the seventh day the child died. David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the child had died, for they said, “While the child was still alive, we spoke to him, and he would not listen to us. How can we tell him that the child has died? He may do something harmful.”
David saw that his servants were whispering, and David realized that the child had died. David said to his servants, “Has the child died?” They said, “He has died.”

Then David rose from the ground, washed, anointed himself, and changed his clothes. He entered the house of God and bowed down before him. Then he went to his own house and asked for bread to eat. They set bread before him, and he ate.
His servants said to him, “What is this that you have done? While the child was alive, you fasted, wept, and kept vigil, but when the child died, you rose, ate, and drank.”
David said, “While the child was alive, I fasted and wept, because I said, ‘Who knows? The Lord may show mercy, and the child may live.’
“But now that the child has died, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me.”
David comforted Bathsheba his wife, went in to her, and slept with her. She conceived and bore a son, and he named him Solomon. The Lord loved him.
He sent word through Nathan the prophet and named him Jedidiah because of the Lord.
Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and came close to taking the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David and said, “I have fought against Rabbah and have come close to taking the city of waters.
“Now gather the rest of your people, encamp against this city, and take it, lest I take the city and it be called by my name.”
David gathered all the people, went to Rabbah, fought against it, and took it.

He took the crown of Milcom, their king, from his head. Its weight was a talent of gold and precious stones, and it was placed on David’s head. He brought out a very great amount of plunder from the city.

He brought out the people who were in it and put them under saws and iron scrapers, and made them pass through the brickworks. He did the same to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and the whole army returned to Jerusalem.
After this, Absalom son of David had a sister who was very beautiful in appearance, whose name was Tamar. Amnon son of David loved her.
Amnon was so distressed over Tamar his sister that he became ill, for she was a virgin, and it seemed difficult to Amnon to do anything to her.
Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, son of Shammah, David’s brother. Jonadab was a very shrewd man.
He said to him, “Why are you growing so thin, son of the king, morning after morning? Will you not tell me?” Amnon said to him, “I love Tamar, the sister of my brother Absalom.”

Jonadab said to him, “Lie down in your bed and pretend to be ill. When your father comes in to see you, say to him, ‘Let my sister Tamar come in and give me gruel. Let her prepare food before my eyes, so that I may see it and eat from her hands.’”
Amnon lay down and became ill, and the king came in to see him. Amnon said to the king, “Let my sister Tamar come to me and prepare some cakes before me, so that I may eat from her hands.”
David sent word to Tamar at home, saying, “Go to the house of your brother Amnon and prepare food for him.”
Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took dough, kneaded it, made cakes before him, and baked the cakes.
She took the pan and emptied it before him, but he refused to eat. Amnon said, “Send everyone out of my presence.” So they sent everyone out of his presence.
Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the food into the bedroom, so that I may eat from your hands.” Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the bedroom to her brother Amnon.
She offered him the food to eat, but he seized her and said to her, “Come, sleep with me, my sister.”
She said to him, “No, my brother! Do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not commit this outrage.
Where would I carry my disgrace? And you would become like one of the wicked fools in Israel. Now speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you.”
But Amnon refused to listen to her. He overpowered her, forced himself on her, violated her, and slept with her.

Then Amnon hated her with an exceedingly great hatred. For the hatred with which he hated her was great, and the suffering that followed was unbearable, greater than the love with which he had first loved her. Amnon said to her, “Get up and go.”
Tamar said to him, “This evil of sending me away is greater than what you have already done to me.” But Amnon refused to listen to her.
He called his young servant, who was in charge of his household, and said to him, “Put this woman out of my presence and shut the door behind her.”
She was wearing an embroidered, long-sleeved robe, for this was how the king’s virgin daughters dressed. The servant put her outside and shut the door behind her.
Tamar took ashes and put them on her head. She tore the long-sleeved robe she was wearing, placed her hands on her head, and went away weeping as she walked.

Her brother Absalom said to her, “Has your brother Amnon been with you? Now, my sister, keep silent, for he is your brother. Do not take it into your mind to speak of this matter.” Tamar lived as a widow in the house of her brother Absalom.
The king heard about these things and became very angry, but he did not upset his son Amnon, because he loved him, for he was his firstborn.
Absalom said nothing to Amnon, either bad or good, because Absalom hated Amnon for having violated his sister Tamar.
After [?] days, Absalom had sheep shearers at Beth-maron, near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king’s sons.
Absalom came to the king and said to him, “Look, your servant has sheep shearers. Let the king and his servants come with your servant.”
The king said to Absalom, “No, my son, let us not all go, so that we do not burden you.” Absalom urged him, but he would not go, and he blessed him.
Absalom said, “If not, at least let my brother Amnon come with me.” The king said, “Why should Amnon go with you?”
Absalom urged him, and he sent Amnon and all the king’s sons with him. Absalom prepared a feast like a king’s feast.

Absalom instructed his servants, saying, “Watch for when Amnon’s heart becomes merry with wine. When I tell you, ‘Strike Amnon and kill him,’ do not be afraid. Am I not the one commanding you? Take courage and be valiant men.”
Absalom’s servants did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded them. Then all the king’s sons rose, each mounted his own mule, and they fled.
While they were on the road, news came to David: “Absalom has slaughtered all the king’s sons and has not left even one of them alive.”
The king rose, tore his clothes, and fell to the ground. All his servants stood around him with their clothes torn.

Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shammah, answered, “Let my lord the king not say that all the king’s sons have died, for only Amnon has died. This had been on Absalom’s lips since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar.
So now, let the king not take this report to heart and say, ‘All the king’s sons have died,’ for only Amnon has died.”

Absalom fled. The young watchman looked up and saw a large crowd coming along the road away from him, down the mountainside. The watchman came and told the king, “I saw men on the road to Horonaim, along the mountainside.”
Jonadab said to the king, “Look, the king’s sons have arrived. It has happened just as your servant said.”
As he finished speaking, the king’s sons arrived. They raised their voices and wept, and the king and all his servants also wept very bitterly.
Absalom fled and went to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur, in the land of Maacah. King David mourned for his son every day.
Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and he stayed there for three years.
King David stopped going out against Absalom, for he had been comforted over Amnon’s death.
Joab son of Zeruiah realized that the king’s heart was set on Absalom.

Joab sent to Tekoa and brought a wise woman from there. He said to her, “Act as a mourner and put on mourning clothes. Do not anoint yourself with oil, but be like a woman who has been mourning for someone long dead.
Go to the king and speak to him in this way.” And Joab put the words in her mouth.
The woman from Tekoa went in to the king, fell facedown on the ground, and said, “Save me, O king, save me!”
The king said to her, “What is the matter with you?” She said, “I am in very great distress. I am a widow; my husband has died.
Your maidservant had two sons. The two fought with each other in the field, and there was no one to intervene between them. One struck the other brother and killed him.

Now the whole family has risen against your servant. They say, ‘Hand over the man who killed his brother, so that we may kill him in return for his brother’s life and do away with your heir.’ They will extinguish the ember I have left, leaving my husband neither a surviving descendant nor a name on the face of the earth.”
The king said, “Go home in peace, and I will give orders concerning you.”
The woman from Tekoa said, “Let the guilt be on me, O king, and on my father’s house, while the king and his throne remain innocent.”
The king said, “Whoever speaks against you, bring him to me, and he will not come near you again.”

She said, “Let the king remember the LORD his God, so that the avenger of blood does not continue destroying and they do not wipe out my little son.” David said, “As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son’s head will fall to the ground.”
The woman said, “Let your servant speak a word before my lord the king.” He said, “Speak.”
The woman said, “Why have you planned such a thing against God’s people? Or does this word from the king’s mouth show him to be at fault, because the king does not bring back the one he has banished?
For one must surely die and, like water poured onto the ground, cannot be gathered up. God will not take a soul, and someone may plan to banish from himself one who has been banished.
Now I have come to speak these words to my lord the king so that the people may see me and say that your servant spoke with the king. Perhaps the king will do what his servant asks.
For the king will listen and rescue me from the hand of the man who seeks to wipe out both me and my son from God’s inheritance.”
And the woman said, “May the word of my lord the king be an offering, for my lord the king is like an angel of God in discerning good and evil. And may the Lord your God be with you.”
The king answered and said to the woman, “Do not hide from me anything I ask you.” And the woman said, “Let my lord the king speak.”

The king said, “Is Joab’s hand with you in all this?” And the woman said to the king, “As you live, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right or to the left from anything my lord the king has said. For your servant Joab instructed me, and he put all these words into the mouth of your servant.
Your servant Joab did these things to change the course of this matter. My lord is wise, with the wisdom of an angel of God, and knows everything that is on the earth.”
The king said to Joab, “Look, I have done for you according to your request. Go and bring back the young man Absalom.”

Joab fell facedown to the ground, bowed before him, and blessed the king. And Joab said, “Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, because my lord the king has granted his servant’s request.”
Joab got up and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
The king said, “Let him return to his own house, but he must not see my face.” So Absalom returned to his own house and did not see the king’s face.
In all Israel there was no man as handsome and highly praised as Absalom. From the soles of his feet to the crown of his head, there was no blemish in him.
He would cut his hair at regular intervals because it grew very heavy on him. When he cut it, he weighed the hair of his head: two hundred shekels by the royal weight standard.
Three sons and one daughter were born to Absalom. Her name was Tamar, and she was very beautiful in appearance. She became the wife of Rehoboam son of Solomon and bore him Abijah.
Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two years and did not see the king’s face.
Absalom sent for Joab to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. He sent for him a second time, but he would not come.

Absalom said to his servants, “You know Joab’s plot of land, full of barley, is near mine. Go and set it on fire.” And Absalom’s servants set Joab’s plot on fire. Joab’s servants came to him with their clothes torn and said, “Absalom’s servants have set the plot on fire.”
Joab got up and came to Absalom at his house and said to him, “Why have your servants set my plot on fire?”

Absalom said to Joab, “I sent for you, saying, ‘Come here, so that I may send you to the king to say, “Why did I come from Geshur? It would have been better for me to remain there than not to see the king’s face. And if there is any guilt in me, kill me.”’”
Joab went in to the king and told him. The king summoned Absalom, and he came in to the king, bowed before him, and fell facedown to the ground before the king. And the king kissed Absalom.
After this, Absalom acquired chariots and horses and fifty men to run ahead of him.

Absalom would rise early and stand beside the road to the gate. Whenever anyone with a case came to the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and say, “What city are you from?” And the man would say, “Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel.”
Absalom said to him, “Look, your claims are good and straightforward, but there is no one appointed by the king to hear you.”
Absalom would say, “If only someone would appoint me judge over this land! Then everyone who had a dispute or a case would come to me, and I would give him justice.”
Whenever a man approached to bow down before him, he would stretch out his hand, draw him close, and kiss him.
Absalom did this to every Israelite who came to the king for judgment, and Absalom drew the hearts of all the men of Israel to himself.
After four years, Absalom said to his father, “Let me go to Hebron and fulfill the vows I made to the Lord.
For your servant made a solemn vow while I was in Geshur in Syria, saying, ‘If the Lord brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the Lord.’”
The king said to him, “Go in peace.” So he arose and went to Hebron.
Absalom sent messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, “When you hear the sound of the horn, say, ‘Absalom has become king in Hebron.’”
Two hundred invited men went with Absalom. They went innocently and knew nothing at all of the matter.
While offering his sacrifices, Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Tekoite, David’s adviser, from his city, Giloh. The gathering grew strong, and many people were joining Absalom.
A messenger came to David with bad news and said, “The hearts of the men of Israel have gone over to Absalom.”

David said to all his servants who were with him in Jerusalem, “Get up, and let us flee, for we cannot escape Absalom. Hurry and leave, lest he quickly overtake us, bring disaster upon us, and strike the city with the edge of the sword.”
The king’s servants said to the king, “Whatever our lord the king wishes, here we are, your servants.”
The king and his entire household went out on foot, and the king left ten women from among his concubines to look after the house.
The king went out, and all his servants went on foot. They stopped beside the olive tree there in the wilderness.
All his servants passed by him one by one, along with all the Cherethites and Pelethites. All the Gittites, six hundred men who had come on foot from Gath, passed before David.
The king said to Ittai the Gittite, “Why should you also come with us? Turn back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner. You left your own place in Gath and came here.
Should I now make you wander with us, when I myself am going wherever I can go? But you should return and take your brothers back with you. May the Lord show you mercy and faithfulness.”
Ittai answered the king, “As the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king may be, whether in death or in life, there your servant will also be.”
The king said to Ittai, “Come, pass by me.” So Ittai the Gittite passed by, together with all his servants and the whole company with him.
The whole land wept loudly, and all the troops were crossing the Kidron Valley. The king also crossed the Kidron Valley, and all the troops and the king went along the road toward the wilderness.

And behold, Zadok and all the Levites with him carried the ark of the Lord’s covenant from Baethar and set down the ark of God. And he went up from Baethar until all the people had finished leaving the city.
The king said to Zadok, “Take the ark of God back into the city, and let it remain in its place. If I find favor before the Lord, he will bring me back and show me it and its beauty.
But if he says to me, ‘I am not pleased with you,’ here I am. Let him do to me whatever is pleasing in his eyes.”
The king said to Zadok the priest, “See that you return to the city in peace, with Ahimaaz your son and Jonathan the son of Abiathar, both your sons, with you.
I will camp in Araboth in the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me.”
So Zadok and Abiathar brought the ark back to Jerusalem, and it remained there.
David went up the slope of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, with his head covered and his feet bare. All the people with him, each with a cloth covering his head, went up weeping.
David was informed, “Ahithophel is among those gathered around Absalom.” David said, “Confound Ahithophel’s counsel, O Lord my God.”
David reached Rosh, where he bowed down to God. There to meet him was Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, with his robe torn and earth on his head.
David said to him, “If you go with me, you will be a burden to me.

But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, ‘Your brothers have gone away, and the king was eagerly pursuing me, and your father has gone away. Now I am your servant, O king; let me stand before you. I was your father’s servant then, and now I am your servant, O king,’ you will confound Ahithophel’s counsel for me.
Zadok and Abiathar the priests are there with you. Whatever you hear from the king’s house, report it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.”
Their two sons are there with them: Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar. Send me through them everything you hear.
Hushai, David’s friend, entered the city as Absalom was entering the city.

David had gone a little beyond Rosh when Ziba, Mephibosheth’s servant, came to meet him with a pair of loaded donkeys carrying two hundred loaves, a hundred raisin cakes, a hundred dates, and a jar of wine.

The king said to Ziba, “What are these for?” Ziba said, “The donkeys are for the king to ride, the bread and dates are food for the young men, and the wine is for those who grow faint here in the wilderness to drink.”
The king said, “Where is your master’s son?” Ziba said to the king, “He is staying in Jerusalem, for he says, ‘Today the house of Israel will restore my father’s kingdom to me.’”
The king said to Ziba, “Everything belonging to Mephibosheth shall now be yours.” Ziba bowed down and said, “I have found favor in your sight, my lord the king.”
King David came to Bahurim, and a man from the family of the house of Saul came out from there. His name was Shimei son of Gera, and he kept cursing as he came out.
He threw stones at David and everyone who was with King David, while all the people and all the warriors were on the king’s right and left.
Shimei said this as he cursed him: “Get out, get out, you bloodstained man, you lawless man!

The Lord has brought back upon you all the bloodshed of the house of Saul, in whose place you became king. The Lord has handed your kingdom over to your son Absalom. He has shown you your troubles, because you are a bloodstained man.”
Abishai son of Zeruiah said to David, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king like this? Let me go over and take off his head.”
The king said, “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Leave him alone; let him curse like this, because the Lord has told him to curse David. Who can say, ‘Why have you done this?’”

David said to Abishai and all his servants, “Look, my own son, who came from my body, seeks my life. How much more, then, this Benjaminite! Leave him alone and let him curse, because the Lord has told him to.
Perhaps the Lord will see my suffering and repay me with good in place of his curses today.”
David and the men with him continued along the road, while Shimei walked near him along the side of the mountain, cursing as he went, throwing stones toward him and scattering earth over him.
The king and all the troops with him arrived exhausted, and they rested there.
Absalom and all Israel entered Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.
When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, “Long live the king!”
Absalom said to Hushai, “Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?”
Hushai said to Absalom, “No, but I will follow the one whom the Lord, this people, and all the men of Israel have chosen. I will belong to him and remain with him.”
“And secondly, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? Just as I served your father, so I will serve you.”
Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give us your advice about what we should do.”

Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Go in to your father’s concubines, whom he left to look after his house. All Israel will hear that you have disgraced your father, and the hands of everyone with you will be strengthened.”
They pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom went in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.
In those former days, the advice Ahithophel gave was as though someone had sought a word from God. Such was all Ahithophel’s advice, both to David and to Absalom.
Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will set out and pursue David tonight.”
I will come upon him at night, when he is weary and his hands have lost their strength. I will terrify him, and the troops who are with him will flee. I will kill only the king.
I will bring all the troops back to you, as a bride returns to her husband. You need seek the life of only one man, and all the troops will be at peace.
The proposal seemed right to Absalom and all the elders of Israel.
Absalom said, “Call Hushai the Archite, and let us hear what he has to say.”
Hushai came to Absalom, and Absalom told him what Ahithophel had said. He said, “Should we do as he says? If not, then you tell us something.”
Hushai said to Absalom, “The advice Ahithophel has given this time is not good.”

Hushai said, “You yourself know your father and his men: they are very mighty and bitter in spirit, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the wilderness and raging in the field. Your father is a warrior and does not let the army rest.”

“Look, he will be hiding on one of the hills or in some other place. When he falls upon them, he will strike first, and whoever hears of it will say, ‘There has been a slaughter among the people following Absalom.’”
“Even a mighty man whose heart is like a lion’s heart will utterly lose courage, for all Israel knows that your father is mighty and that those with him are mighty warriors.”
“This is the advice I give you: let all the men of Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as numerous as the sand on the seashore, and go among them yourself.”
“We will come upon him in whatever place we find him, and surround him as dew falls upon the ground. We will leave none of his men alive, not one.”
“If he enters a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will drag them down to the ravine, so that not even one stone remains there.”

Absalom and all the men of Israel said, “The advice of Hushai the Archite is better than Ahithophel’s advice.” The Lord had commanded that Ahithophel’s good advice be frustrated, so that the Lord might bring every disaster upon Absalom.
Hushai the Archite said to the priests Zadok and Abiathar, “Ahithophel gave such and such advice to Absalom and the elders of Israel, and I advised such and such.”
“Now send quickly and tell David, ‘Do not spend tonight at Araboth in the wilderness, but hurry to cross over, lest the king and all the people with him be swallowed up.’”
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying by the spring of En-rogel. A servant girl went and told them, and they went and reported this to King David, for they could not enter the city and be seen there.
A young man saw them and told Absalom. The two of them went and entered the house of a man in Bahurim. He had a well in his house, and they went down into it.
The woman took a cover and spread it over the well, and she was drying [?] on top of it. The matter did not become known.

Absalom’s servants came to the woman at the house and said, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” The woman said to them, “They have gone beyond that water.” They searched for them but did not find them, and returned to Jerusalem.
After they had gone, the men came up out of the well and went and told King David. They said to David, “Get up and cross the water, for Ahithophel has planned this and that against you.”
David and all the people with him rose and crossed the Jordan. By daybreak, not a single person remained who had not crossed the Jordan.

When Ahithophel saw that his advice had not been followed, he saddled his donkey and set out for his home in his city. He gave instructions to his household, hanged himself, and died. He was buried in his father’s tomb.
David reached Mahanaim, and Absalom crossed the Jordan with all Israel.
Absalom appointed Amasa over the army in place of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Jether the Jezreelite, who had slept with Abigail, the daughter of Jesse and sister of Zeruiah, Joab’s mother.
Absalom and all Israel camped in the land of Gilead.
When David reached Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim
brought ten beds, blankets, ten cooking pots, earthenware vessels, wheat, barley, flour, roasted-grain flour, peas, and lentils,
and honey, butter, [?], and suckling calves. They presented these to David and the army with him to eat, because the army was hungry, thirsty, and exhausted there in the wilderness.
David mustered the army with him and appointed commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds over them.

David sent out a third of the army under Joab, a third under Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third under Ittai the Gittite. David said to the army, “I myself will certainly go out with you.”

They said, “You must not go out. If we flee, they will pay no attention to us, and if half of us die, they will pay no attention to us. But you are worth ten thousand of us. So it is better for you to stay in the city, so that you can help us.”
The king said to them, “I will do whatever seems good to you.” The king stood leaning by the gate, and the whole army went out by hundreds and thousands.
The king gave orders to Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, saying, “Spare my young man Absalom.” All the troops heard the king giving orders to all the commanders concerning Absalom.
The whole army went out into the forest against Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim.
The troops of Israel were defeated there by David’s servants. There was a great slaughter that day, and twenty thousand men fell.
The battle there spread over the whole countryside, and that day the forest devoured more of the army than the sword did.

Absalom encountered David’s servants. Absalom was riding his mule, and the mule went beneath a large, thick oak. His head became caught in the oak, and he hung between heaven and earth while the mule passed on beneath him.
A man saw him and reported it to Joab, saying, “Look, I saw Absalom hanging from the oak.”
Joab said to the man who told him, “You saw him? Why did you not strike him down to the ground? I would have given you fifty shekels of silver and a sword today.”

The man said to Joab, “Even if I received a thousand shekels of silver weighed out from your hands, I would not raise my hand against the king’s son. For in our hearing the king commanded you, Abishai, and Ittai, saying, ‘Be careful with the young man Absalom.’
Do him no harm. Nothing will be hidden from the king, and you would stand aside.”
Joab said, “For that very reason, I will go on ahead of you.” Joab took three darts in his hand and thrust them into Absalom’s heart while he was still alive in the oak tree.
Ten young men from among Joab’s armor-bearers surrounded Absalom, struck him, and killed him.
Joab blew the horn, and the army with him turned back so that they would no longer pursue Israel, for Joab spared the army.
And Joab took Absalom and threw him into a great pit in the forest, very deep, and all Israel fled, each man to his own home.

But while Absalom was still alive, he erected a monument for himself and set up the monuments in Jabin, in the Valley of the Kings, for he said that he had no son to preserve the memory of his name. He named the monument after himself, and it has been called Absalom’s Monument to this day.
And Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, “Let me run and bring the king good news, for the Lord has vindicated him against his enemies.”
And Joab said to him, “You are not the man to bring good news today. You may bring good news another day, but today do not bring good news, because the king’s son has died.”
And he said to Cushi, “Go, tell the king whatever you have seen.” And Cushi bowed down before Joab and departed.

And Ahimaaz son of Zadok spoke again and said to Joab, “What would it matter if I too ran after Cushi?” And Joab said, “Why should you run, my son? Come here. The news will bring you no benefit from going.”
And Ahimaaz said, “What would it matter if I ran?” And Joab said to him, “Run.” And Ahimaaz ran along the road through Kikkar and overtook Cushi.
And David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman went up onto the roof of the gate, on the wall, raised his eyes, and looked, and there was a man running alone toward him.
And the watchman called out and informed the king, and the king said, “If he is alone, there is good news in his mouth.” And the man kept coming and drew near.
And the watchman saw another man running, and the watchman called down to the gate and said, “There is another man running alone.” And the king said, “He too is bringing good news.”
And the watchman said, “I see that the first man runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok.” And the king said, “He is a good man, and he comes with good news.”

And Ahimaaz called out and said to the king, “All is well!” And he bowed down with his face to the ground and said, “Blessed is the Lord your God, who has trapped the men who hate you, who raised their hands against our lord the king.”
And the king said, “Is my young son Absalom well?” And Ahimaaz said, “I saw a great crowd when Joab, your servant, O king, sent me, your servant, but I did not know what was happening there.”
And the king said, “Turn aside and stand there.” And he turned aside and stood there.
And Cushi arrived and said to the king, “Good news for my lord the king! For today the Lord has vindicated you against all who rose against you.”
And the king said to Cushi, “Is my young son Absalom well?” And Cushi said, “May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise against you to do you harm, become like that young man.”

And the king was deeply distressed and went up to the upper room over the gate and wept. And as he wept he said, “My son Absalom, Absalom my son! If only I had died in your place—I in your place, Absalom my son, my son Absalom!”
And Joab was told, “Look, the king is weeping and mourning over Absalom.”
And the victory that day became mourning for the whole army, because that day the army heard people saying, “The king is grieving for his son.”
And that day the army was reluctant to enter the city, as an army is reluctant when it is ashamed after fleeing from battle.
And the king covered his face and wailed loudly, saying, “My son Absalom, Absalom my son!”

And Joab went into the house to the king and said, “Today you have shamed all your servants, who today saved your life and the lives of your sons and daughters, and the lives of your wives and concubines.”

You love those who hate you and hate those who love you. Today you have shown that you think nothing of your commanders or your servants. Today I know for certain that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead, that would please you.

“Now get up, go out, and speak to the hearts of your servants. For I swear by the Lord that if you do not go out today, not one man will stay with you tonight. And know for yourself that this will be worse for you than all the troubles that have come upon you from your youth until now.”

The king rose and sat at the gate. They told the whole army, saying, “Look, the king is sitting at the gate.” Then the whole army came before the king, while the Israelites fled, each man to his own home.

All the people throughout all the tribes of Israel were troubled and said, “King David rescued us from all our enemies and saved us from the hands of the Philistines. But now he has fled from the land and from his kingdom because of Absalom.”
“Absalom, whom we anointed over us, has died in battle. Now why do you remain silent about bringing the king back?”

The message of all Israel came to the king. King David sent word to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, saying, “Speak to the elders of Judah and say, ‘Why are you the last to bring the king back to his house?’” And the message of all Israel came to the king.
David said to the tribe of Judah, “You are my bones and my flesh. Why are you the last to bring the king back to his house?”
“And say to Amasa, ‘Are you not my bone and my flesh? May God do this and that to me, and add this and that, if you do not become commander of the army before me for all time in place of Joab.’”
He turned the hearts of all Judah as though they were one man. They sent word to the king, saying, “Return, you and all your servants.”
The king returned and came as far as the Jordan. The men of Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and bring him across the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, son of Jemini, from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
With him were a thousand men from Benjamin, and Ziba, the servant of Saul’s household, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants. They made the Jordan ready before the king.

They carried out the service of bringing the king across, and the ferrymen crossed over to rouse the king’s household and show kindness in his sight. Shimei son of Gera fell on his face before the king as he was crossing the Jordan.
He said to the king, “Let my lord the king not count wrongdoing against me, nor remember the offense your servant committed on the day my lord left Jerusalem, taking it to heart.
For your servant knows that I have sinned. Look, I have come today before all the house of Joseph to come down and meet my lord the king.”
Abishai son of Zeruiah answered and said, “Should Shimei not be put to death for this, because he cursed the Lord’s anointed?”

David said, “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah, that you should act treacherously toward me today? Let no man in Israel be put to death today. Do I not know that today I am king over Israel?”
The king said to Shimei, “You will not die.” And the king swore an oath to him.

Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came down to meet the king. He had not tended his feet, cut his nails, trimmed his beard, attended to his mustache, or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he returned in peace.
When he entered Jerusalem, he came out to meet the king. The king said to him, “Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?”

Mephibosheth said to him, “My lord the king, my servant treated me with contempt. For your servant said to him, ‘Saddle a donkey for me, so that I may ride it and go with the king,’ because your servant is lame.
Your servant made you angry with me, my lord the king. My lord the king did what was good in his own sight, like an angel of God. Now do whatever is good in your eyes.

For all my father’s household were nothing but men deserving death before my lord the king, yet you placed your servant among those who eat at the king’s table. What right do I have now to make any further complaint to the king?”
The king said to him, “Why do you keep speaking about your affairs? I have said that you and Ziba are to divide the estate.”
Mephibosheth said to the king, “Let him take it all, since the king has returned to his house in peace.”
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and accompanied the king across the Jordan to see him off from the Jordan.
Barzillai was a very old man, eighty years old. He had provided food for the king while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man.
The king said to Barzillai, “Cross over with me, and I will provide for you in your old age with me in Jerusalem.”
Barzillai said to the king, “How many days of my life remain, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?”

“I am eighty years old today. Can I discern anything between good and bad? Can your servant taste what I eat or drink? Can I still hear the voices of male and female singers? Why should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?
Your servant has crossed the Jordan only a little way with the king. Why should the king repay me with this reward?

Let your servant stay and die in his own city, at the tomb of his father and mother. Here is your servant Chimham; let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good in your eyes.”
The king said, “Let Chimham cross over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good in my eyes. Whatever you ask of me, I will do for you.”
All the people crossed the Jordan, and the king crossed over too. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own place.
The king crossed over to Gilgal, and Chimham crossed over with him. All the people of Judah and half the people of Israel crossed over with the king.
Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to him, “Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought the king and his household across the Jordan?”
