The men of Judah answered the men of Israel and said, “Because the king is closely related to us. Why are you displeased about this? Have we eaten anything at the king’s expense? Has he given us a gift, or has he carried any burden of ours?”

The men of Israel answered the men of Judah and said, “We have ten shares in the king, and we are the firstborn compared with you. In David too, we have a greater share than you. Why have you insulted us like this? Was not our proposal to bring the king back to us made first?” But the words of the men of Judah were harsher than the words of the men of Israel.

There a lawless man named Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite, grew bold. He blew a horn and said, “We have no share in David and no inheritance in the son of Jesse. Israel, let every man go to his own dwelling!”
All Israel left David and followed Sheba son of Bichri, but the men of Judah followed their king from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

David entered his house in Jerusalem. The king took the ten women, his concubines whom he had left to guard the house, and put them in a house under guard. He provided food for them but did not sleep with them. They were confined and lived as widows until the day of their death.
David said to Amasa, “Summon all the men of Judah to me within three days, and come here yourself.”
Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the time appointed for him.

David said to Abishai, “Now Sheba son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord’s servants with you and pursue him vigorously, lest he find fortified cities for himself and cast a shadow over our eyes.”
Abishai, Joab’s men, the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty warriors went out after him. They left Jerusalem to pursue Sheba son of Bichri vigorously.
While they were at the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa came before them. Joab was wearing an armored cloak, and over it a sword was fastened at his waist, together with its sheath. It was partly drawn.
Joab said to Amasa, “Are you well, brother?” Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.

Amasa did not guard against the sword in Joab’s hand. Joab struck him with it in the belly, and his entrails poured out onto the ground. He did not strike him again, and Amasa died. Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba son of Bichri vigorously.
A man from among Joab’s young men came and stood over Amasa and said, “Whoever loves Joab or David should follow Joab and Abishai.”

Amasa lay drenched in blood in the middle of the road. When the man saw that the whole army had stopped, he threw Amasa off the road into a field and threw a garment over him, because he saw that everyone who came along stopped over him.
When he had been removed from the road, every man of Israel went on after Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.
He passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel and Beth-maacah, and all the specially chosen men gathered and came after him.

They arrived and besieged him in Abel and Beth-maacah. They piled up a mound of earth facing the city, and it stood like a rampart. All the troops with Joab were breaking down and demolishing the wall.
A wise woman cried out from the wall and said, “Listen! Listen! Tell Joab, ‘Come here, and I will speak with you.’”
He approached her, and the woman said, “Are you Joab?” He said, “I am.” She said to him, “Listen to the words of your servant.” Joab said, “I have come to listen.”

She spoke and said, “In former times a saying was repeated: ‘They made careful inquiries in Abel and in Dan whether the faithful of Israel would destroy or plunder. They should make careful inquiries in Abel, and then whether they would destroy [?].’”
“I am a peacemaker for the security of Israel, and you seek to destroy the cities of Israel. Why are you swallowing up the Lord’s inheritance?”
Joab answered and said, “Far be it from me! Far be it from me to swallow up and destroy!

That is not the situation. A man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Sheba son of Bichri, has raised his hand against King David. Give me him alone, and I will leave this city.” The woman said to Joab, “Look, his head will be thrown to you over the wall.”

The woman went to all the people and spoke to the whole city with her wisdom, urging them to cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri. They cut it off and threw it to Joab. He blew the horn, and they dispersed from that city, each man to his own home. Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
Joab was over the whole army of Israel, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites.
Adoniram was over the tribute, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
Sheva was the chief scribe, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Ira the Jairite was also David’s priest.

There was a famine in the days of David for three years, one year after another. David sought the Lord’s presence, and the Lord said, “This calamity is because of Saul and the bloodshed of his house, because he slaughtered the Gibeonites.”

King David summoned the Gibeonites and spoke to them. The Gibeonites were not Israelites but descendants of the Amorites, and the Israelites had sworn an oath to them. Saul had sought to strike them down in his zeal for the Israelites and Judah.
David said to the Gibeonites, “What shall I do for you, and how shall I make atonement, so that you may bless the Lord’s inheritance?”
The Gibeonites said to him, “We have no claim for silver or gold against Saul or his house, nor do we want any man in Israel put to death.” He said, “Then what do you say I should do for you?”
They said to the king, “The man who devastated us and persecuted us, who planned to wipe us out—let us destroy him, so that he may no longer remain anywhere within the borders of Israel.”
Let seven men from among his sons be given to us, and we will hang them up before the Lord in Gibeah of Saul, the Lord’s chosen one. The king said, “I will give them to you.”
The king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, because of the oath before the Lord between Jonathan son of Saul and David.

The king took the two sons of Rizpah daughter of Aiah, whom she had borne to Saul, Armoni and Ish-bosheth, and the five sons of Merab daughter of Saul, whom she had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.

And he handed them over to the Gibeonites, and they hung them on the mountain before the Lord. All seven fell there together, and they died in the first days of harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

And Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it over them on the rock, from the beginning of the barley harvest until water fell on them from heaven. She did not allow the birds of heaven to settle on them by day, or the wild beasts of the wilderness by night.
And David was told what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul’s concubine, had done. And they grew weary, and Dan son of Joash, a descendant of the giants, came upon them.

And David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the squares of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had displayed them on the day when the Philistines struck them down at Gilboa.
And he brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan.

He also gathered those who had been hung, in the land of Benjamin, at the tomb near Kish, his father. And they were buried there, and they did everything the king commanded. After this, God heeded the land.
And once again there was war between the Philistines and Israel. David went down with his servants, and they fought against the Philistines, and David grew weary.
And Abishai at Jesbe, who was a descendant of Rapha, whose spear weighed three hundred shekels of solid bronze, and who wore a sword at his waist, intended to strike David.

And Abishai son of Zeruiah helped David and struck the Philistine and killed him. Then David’s men swore to him, saying, “You shall no longer go out to battle with us, so that you do not extinguish the lamp of Israel.”
And after this there was once again war at Gath against the Philistines. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, a descendant of Rapha.
And once again there was war at Rob against the Philistines. Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver’s beam.
And once again there was war at Gath. There was a man there named Maon, with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. He too was born to Rapha.
And he taunted Israel, and Jonathan son of Shammah, David’s brother, struck him down.
These four were born to Rapha in his house at Gath, and they fell by the hands of David and by the hands of his servants.
And David spoke the words of this blessing to the Lord on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hands of all his enemies and from the hands of Saul.
And he said, “The Lord is my rock, my stronghold, and my deliverer.
God will be my guardian; I will trust in him. He is my protector and the horn of my salvation, my defender and my refuge of salvation. You will deliver me from injustice, Lord.
I will call upon the Lord, who is worthy of praise, and I will be saved from my enemies.
For the crushing blows of death surrounded me; torrents of lawlessness distressed me.
The pangs of death surrounded me; the snares of death came upon me.
In my distress I called upon the Lord, and I will cry out to my God. From his holy temple he will hear my voice, and my cry will reach his ears.
He looked, and the earth was troubled and shook. The foundations of heaven were troubled and overturned, because the Lord was angry with them.
Smoke rose from his anger, and fire from his mouth will consume; burning coals were kindled by him.
And he lowered the heavens and came down, and thick darkness was beneath his feet.
He went up and sat upon the cherubim and flew, and he appeared upon the wings of the winds.
And he made darkness his covering, his tent around him, and the darkness of the waters thickened the clouds of the air.
From the brightness before him, sparks of fire blazed.
And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice.
And he sent his arrows and scattered them; he flashed his lightning and terrified them.
And the torrents of the sea appeared, and the foundations of the world were revealed at the Lord’s rebuke and at the blast of the wind of his anger.
He reached down from on high and took me; he drew me out of many waters.
He snatched me from the oppression of my enemies and from those who hated me, for they were stronger than I.
The days of my distress came upon me, and the Lord became my support.
And he brought me out to safety and rescued me, because he was pleased with me.
And the Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness, and according to the purity of my hands the Lord will repay me.
For I kept the ways of the Lord and did not wickedly turn away from my God.
For all his judgments are before me, and I did not depart from his righteous ordinances.
And I will be blameless before him, and I will take precautions against my wrongdoing.
And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness and according to the purity of my hands before his eyes.
With the holy you will be holy, and with the perfect man you will be perfect.
And with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the crooked you will be crooked.
For you will save the poor people and bring down the eyes of the proud.
For you are my lamp, Lord, and you, Lord, will light up my darkness.
For with you I will run lightly armed, and with my God I will pass over a wall.
My mighty God, whose way is blameless—the Lord’s mighty word is tested; he watches over all who take refuge in him.
Who is mighty except you, Lord, and who is a sustainer except our God?
The Mighty One, who strengthens me with power, has made my way blameless.
To make my feet like a deer’s; and he sets me upon the heights.
He trains my hands for war and has made my arms firm as a bronze bow.
And you gave me the protection of my salvation, and my obedience made me great.
Room beneath my steps, and my ankles did not falter.
I will pursue my enemies and destroy them, and I will not return until I have consumed them.
I will crush them, and they shall not rise; they shall fall beneath my feet.
You will strengthen me with power for battle and bring those who rise against me down beneath me.
You turned my enemies back before me and destroyed those who hate me.
They will cry out, but there will be no one to help; they will cry to the Lord, but he did not hear them.
I ground them like the dust of the earth, and I will crush them like mud in the streets.
You will rescue me from the strife of peoples and preserve me as the head of nations. A people I did not know served me, and as soon as they heard, they obeyed me.
Foreigners lied to me, and as soon as they heard, they obeyed me.
Foreigners will fall away and stumble out of their strongholds.
The Lord lives, and blessed is my Guardian. May my God, the guardian of my salvation, be exalted.
The mighty Lord, who exacts vengeance, disciplines peoples beneath me.
He brings me out from my enemies. You will exalt me above those who rise against me; you will rescue me from the unjust man.
Therefore I will give thanks to you among the nations, Lord, and sing praises to your name.
He grants great salvation to the king and shows mercy to his anointed, to David and his descendants forever.
These are David’s last words: Faithful is David, the son of Jesse, and faithful is the man whom the Lord appointed as God’s anointed over Jacob, and pleasing are the songs of Israel.
The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me, and his word was on my tongue.
The God of Israel speaks to me, and the Guardian of Israel spoke: I spoke a parable to a man: Who will hold fast to the fear of the Lord and of God in the morning light?
The sun rose in the morning and did not fade in its light, and like green growth from the earth after rain.
For my house is not so with the mighty God. He established an everlasting covenant for me, ready to be kept at all times, for the Lord is all my salvation and all my desire.
For the lawless must not sprout; they are all cast away like thorns that cannot be picked up by hand.
A man will toil among them, and he will burn all the iron and the spear shaft with fire, and they will blaze in their shame.
These are the names of David’s commanders: Jebosthe the Canaanite, commander of the [?] division; Adino the Eznite, over eight hundred slain in a single encounter.

After him was Elhanan, the son of his uncle, the son of the Sobaite, one of David’s three commanders at Ramah, when he taunted the Philistines, where they had gathered for battle; and a man of Israel took courage.
He rose and struck down the Philistines until his hand clung to the sword. The Lord brought about a great deliverance that day, and the army stayed behind him, except to take the plunder.
After him was Shammah, the son of Sisa, the Aruchite. The Philistines gathered at Lehi, and there was a plot of land there full of lentils. The army fled before the Philistines.
He stood firm in the middle of the plot and saved it, and he struck down the Philistines. The Lord brought about a great deliverance.
Three of the thirty went down, and they went down to Kasoba, to David in the cave of Adullam. Bands of Philistines were encamped in the valleys of the Rephaim.
David was then in the stronghold, and the Philistine camp was then in Bethlehem.
David longed for water and said, “Oh, who would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!”

The Philistine troops were in Bethlehem. Three commanders broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well of Bethlehem by the gate, took it, and brought it to David. But he would not drink it; instead, he offered it to the Lord.
He said, “Far be it from me, Lord, to do this! Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?” And he would not drink it. These things the three commanders did.
Abishai, the brother of Joab, son of Zeruiah, was chief among the three. He raised his spear against three hundred wounded men, and he had a name among the three.
He was honored above them and became their chief, but he did not attain the rank of the three.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the son of a mighty man who had done many deeds in Kabzeel, struck down the two sons of Ariel the Moabite. He also went down and killed the lion in the pit on a snowy day.

He also killed a distinguished man, an Egyptian. The Egyptian held a spear like a bridge beam. He went down against him with a spear, snatched the spear from the Egyptian’s hands, and killed him with his own spear.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada did these things, and he had a name among the three mighty men.
He was honored above the three, but he did not attain the rank of the three. David appointed him over his storehouses.
These are the names of King David’s mighty men: Asahel the brother of Joab, who was among the thirty; Elhanan son of Ahihud, his uncle, in Bethlehem;
Shammah the Rudite; Shallum the Kelothite;
Helez the Paltite; Ira son of Ikkesh, the Tekoite.
Abiezer the Anathothite, from the sons of the Asothite;
Ellon the Ahohite; Noere the Netophathite;
Aghap son of Pamphanai; Anaove the Nephlatite; Ittai son of Ribai, in Gibeah of the sons of
Benjamin; the Ephrathite; Addai from the valley of Govasa;
Abi-albon from the plains; Addai from Nakhalah; Gasbiah the Gadabarite; Asmon the Barasamite;
Elijah the Shaalbonite; Jonathan son of Asana;
Shamnan the Arovdite; Elian son of Ared, the Arathirite;
Eliphelet son of the Asibite, son of Maacah; Eliab son of Ahithophel the Galamonite;
Asare the Carmelite; Tuur the Erkite;
Gala son of Nathan, from the army, son of Gilead;
Eli the Ammonite; Gelovre the Beerothite, the quiver-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah;
Ira the Ithrite; Gareb the Bethanite; Uriah the Hittite.
Thirty-seven in all; others from the ravine of Gadabiel, son of the Arabothite.
The Lord’s anger again burned against Israel, and he stirred David up against them, saying, “Go, count Israel and Judah.”
The king said to Joab, the commander of the army who was with him, “Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and count the people, so that I may know their number.”
Joab said to the king, “May the Lord increase the people a hundredfold, however many they are, and may the eyes of my lord the king see it. But why does my lord the king desire this thing?”
But the king’s command prevailed over Joab and the commanders of the army. Joab and all the commanders of the army went out from the king’s presence to count the people of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan and went around Aroer, to the right of the city in the valley of Gad and Eleazar.
They passed through Gilead, to Tabason, Esthon, and Adase, and reached Dan. Then they went around Sidon.
They came to Mapsar of Tyre and to all the cities of the Hivites and the Canaanites, and they came from the southern side to Judah and to Beersheba.
They went around the whole land and arrived in Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.
Joab gave the king the total from the count of the people. In Israel there were eight hundred thousand fighting men who drew the sword, and the men of Judah numbered five hundred thousand warriors.

David’s heart struck him after he had counted the people. David said to the Lord, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done. Now take away your servant’s wrongdoing, for I have acted very foolishly.”
David rose in the morning, and the word of the Lord came to Gad the prophet, David’s seer, saying:
“Go and speak to David, and say, ‘This is what the Lord says: I offer you three things. Choose one of them for yourself, and I will do it to you.’”

Gad came to David, told him, and said to him, “Choose for yourself whether three years of famine shall come upon your land, or you shall flee for three months before your enemies while they pursue you, or there shall be three days of death in your land. Now consider and see what answer I should give to the one who sent me.”

David said to Gad, “I am in great danger on every side. But now let me fall into the hands of the Lord, for his mercies are very great, and let me not fall into human hands.” David chose the plague for himself, and it was the time of the wheat harvest.
The Lord sent a plague upon Israel from morning until midday, and the destruction began among the people. Seventy thousand men died among the people, from Dan to Beersheba.

The angel of God stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it. But the Lord relented concerning the calamity and said to the angel who was destroying the people, “Enough! Now withdraw your hand.” The angel of the Lord was beside the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When David saw the angel striking the people, he said to the Lord, “Here I am: I have sinned. I, the shepherd, have done wrong. But these sheep—what have they done? Let your hand be against me and my father’s household.”
Gad came to David that day and said to him, “Go up and erect an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”
David went up according to Gad’s word, as the Lord had commanded him.
Araunah bowed when he saw the king and his servants coming toward him. He went out to him and bowed before his lord with his face to the ground.
Araunah said, “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” David said, “To buy the threshing floor from you and build an altar to the Lord, so that the destruction among the people may stop.”

Araunah said to David, “Let my lord the king take it and offer to the Lord whatever is pleasing in his sight. Here are the oxen for a burnt offering, and the wheels and the oxen’s equipment for firewood.”
Araunah gave everything to the king, and Araunah said to the king, “May the Lord your God bless you.”

The king said to Araunah, “No, but I will buy it from you for a price. I will not offer the Lord my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.

David built an altar there to the Lord God and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings upon it. Solomon later enlarged the altar, because it was small at first. The Lord answered the land’s plea, and the destruction was stopped in Israel.
